Name: Pool Model (Shared Everything)
Strategy: Shared compute and storage with enforced tenant scope on every tenant-owned access path; shared SQL tables commonly use tenant_id
Strengths: Efficient resource utilization; centralized deployment and operations
Weaknesses: Shared capacity and outage exposure; isolation must cover APIs and storage as well as SQL
When to Use: Cost-sensitive SaaS where logical isolation satisfies workload and contractual requirements
Gotcha: A tenant column or network boundary alone does not isolate pooled data; authorize tenant context and use constrained database roles and tested policies; include background and administrative paths

Name: Silo Model (Shared Nothing)
Strategy: Dedicated tenant resource stack with enforced identity and access boundaries
Strengths: Reduces tenant workload contention and blast radius; enables independent sizing and recovery
Weaknesses: Higher cost and fleet-management overhead; shared control planes and regional dependencies still need analysis
When to Use: Tenants requiring dedicated resources or independently managed capacity and recovery
Gotcha: Separate schemas or databases on one shared server are not a full silo; automate provisioning and verify cross-stack access denial; isolation alone does not establish compliance

Name: Bridge Model (Hybrid)
Strategy: Combine pooled and siloed resources by service or tier; document tenant routing and access boundaries for each component
Strengths: Targets dedicated capacity or data boundaries where required while retaining some pooling benefits
Weaknesses: Multiple deployment and migration paths; shared components still carry contention and isolation risks
When to Use: Workloads with differing isolation requirements across services or tenant tiers
Gotcha: Hybrid is not limited to shared compute plus separate databases; a separate schema is not dedicated capacity; validate routing and all replica and export locations before claiming residency

Name: Row-Level Security (RLS)
Strategy: Enable PostgreSQL RLS on tenant tables; use USING for visible rows and WITH CHECK for new row values
Strengths: Default deny when enabled without an applicable policy; defense against omitted tenant filters
Weaknesses: Superusers and BYPASSRLS roles bypass policies; owners normally bypass unless FORCE ROW LEVEL SECURITY; permissive policies combine with OR
When to Use: Pooled PostgreSQL data accessed through a non-owner application role without BYPASSRLS
Gotcha: FORCE does not constrain superusers or BYPASSRLS; TRUNCATE and REFERENCES are outside RLS; integrity checks bypass RLS and can leak existence; audit privileged functions and test reads and writes as the runtime role

Name: Noisy Neighbor Mitigation
Strategy: Apply tenant-aware concurrency and queue budgets plus request and query-cost limits at measured bottlenecks; retain global capacity guards
Strengths: Reduces contention; protects quiet tenants when combined with capacity planning and selective isolation
Weaknesses: HTTP rate limits do not bound CPU or database work; simultaneous compliant tenants can still exhaust shared capacity
When to Use: Shared worker fleets and databases with variable request cost or bursty tenant demand
Gotcha: Load-test one noisy tenant alongside quiet tenants and monitor their latency and queue age; bound query duration and fan-out; offer dedicated capacity when shared-resource SLOs cannot be met

Name: Per-Tenant Rate Limiting
Strategy: Key limits by server-authorized tenant and operation; combine tenant burst and sustained budgets with global and abuse controls
Strengths: Supports tier entitlements and reduces overload when enforcement matches the required guarantees
Weaknesses: Distributed coordination or budget partitioning is needed for aggregate limits; local counters multiply allowance across replicas
When to Use: Multi-tenant APIs with shared capacity or contractual quotas
Gotcha: Define limiter outage behavior and test concurrent replicas; Redis is optional; API Gateway usage-plan quotas are best effort and API keys are not authentication; use atomic admission accounting when a hard cap is required

Name: Tenant-Aware Caching
Strategy: Build collision-resistant keys from authorized tenant context plus resource and response-varying authorization scope; scope invalidation to that namespace
Strengths: Avoids accidental tenant key collisions; supports tenant-scoped lifecycle management
Weaknesses: Prefixes alone enforce no authorization or memory quota; shared cache CPU and eviction permit noisy neighbors
When to Use: Shared caches containing tenant-specific or permission-sensitive data
Gotcha: Authorize cache hits as well as misses; shared credentials can access other prefixes; use supported key-pattern ACLs with tenant-scoped identities or dedicated instances for stronger isolation

Name: Tenant Onboarding Automation
Strategy: Orchestrate tenant identity and resource provisioning with durable progress and retry-safe steps; activate only after access-boundary checks
Strengths: Repeatable provisioning for self-service and provider-managed onboarding; reduced manual configuration drift
Weaknesses: Partial failures can leave orphaned resources or incomplete permissions; reconciliation and rollback need explicit ownership
When to Use: Repeatable SaaS onboarding in pool or dedicated deployments; no universal tenant-count threshold
Gotcha: Use a stable tenant-scoped provisioning key and reconcile uncertain outcomes before retrying; keep failed tenants inactive and test recovery after each provisioning step

Name: Tenant Data Export and Portability
Strategy: Define authorized export scope and deliver documented machine-readable data securely; distinguish organizational migration from individual portability rights
Strengths: Enables contractual migration and applicable personal-data portability; makes export scope explicit
Weaknesses: Related-person data and multiple stores complicate scope; legal applicability depends on jurisdiction and processing basis
When to Use: Contractual tenant exports and applicable data-subject portability requests
Gotcha: UK GDPR Article 20 guidance covers provided personal data processed automatically under consent or contract rather than all company data; protect others' rights and verify recipient authority; document omissions and consistency boundaries

Name: Schema-Per-Tenant
Strategy: Separate tenant namespaces in one database with explicit schema and object privileges
Strengths: Separates object names; allows independently versioned tenant schemas
Weaknesses: Shared database resources and failure domain; migration fan-out; roles with broad grants can access multiple schemas
When to Use: Workloads needing namespace separation where shared capacity and database-level recovery are acceptable
Gotcha: search_path selects names but is not authorization; exclude untrusted writable schemas and revoke inappropriate CREATE privileges including public on older upgraded databases; schema-qualified access still needs grants checked

Name: Tenant-Aware Logging and Observability
Strategy: Attach verified tenant context to tenant-scoped logs and traces; budget metric label cardinality and restrict telemetry access
Strengths: Supports isolation incident investigation and tenant SLO analysis without tagging every global infrastructure event
Weaknesses: Unbounded tenant labels multiply series across endpoints and instances; detailed logs require retention and access controls
When to Use: Shared services requiring tenant diagnostics and resource-use attribution
Gotcha: Recording rules do not remove already-ingested raw series; aggregate before ingestion or use bounded dimensions and a separate tenant analytics store; sampled traces are not an exact billing ledger

Name: Cross-Tenant Analytics
Strategy: Separate authorized platform analytics from tenant-visible benchmark releases; evaluate disclosure risk before releasing aggregates
Strengths: Enables platform insights and reviewed benchmark products; differential privacy can quantify privacy loss
Weaknesses: Small groups and linked releases may expose confidential information; privacy techniques trade accuracy for protection
When to Use: Explicitly authorized platform analysis or externally shared statistics with a documented privacy review
Gotcha: Precomputation or removing identifiers does not prove anonymity; define the protected entity and evaluate the actual differential-privacy guarantee when used; do not promise zero re-identification risk

Name: Verified Tenant Context
Strategy: Resolve tenant selection against authenticated identity and current membership or service scope before any tenant-owned operation
Strengths: Blocks tenant-header spoofing and object access outside authorized tenant scope
Weaknesses: Membership revocation and cross-service propagation need explicit policy; opaque identifiers alone do not authorize access
When to Use: APIs and services where a principal can select one or more tenants
Gotcha: Reject missing or unauthorized tenant context; check resource ownership on each path; explicitly authorize and audit platform-wide jobs instead of silently falling back to an unscoped query

Name: Transaction-Scoped Tenant Context
Strategy: Begin a transaction and set server-verified tenant context with SET LOCAL or transaction-local set_config before dependent queries
Strengths: Prevents committed session settings from leaking tenant selection across pooled requests when context is re-established every transaction
Weaknesses: Requires explicit transactions and fail-closed policies; an application-writable setting is not protection from arbitrary SQL under that role
When to Use: PostgreSQL RLS policies that read tenant identity from a custom setting on reused connections
Gotcha: Set context inside the same transaction as queries; reject missing or invalid context and commit or roll back before release; test tenant A then B plus error and cancellation paths on the same pooled session

Name: Tenant-Aware Async Fairness
Strategy: Bind trusted tenant context to queued work and authorize it at the consumer; use tenant-aware scheduling and bounded worker concurrency
Strengths: Reduces noisy-tenant backlog impact and preserves authorization through delayed execution
Weaknesses: Queue fairness does not enforce data isolation or hard resource quotas; delayed permissions and duplicate deliveries need handling
When to Use: Shared background workers processing bursty or unequal-cost tenant jobs
Gotcha: SQS standard fair queues use MessageGroupId as tenant identity without FIFO ordering or per-tenant rate caps; scope deduplication and retries by tenant and monitor quiet-tenant dwell time

Name: Tenant Export Snapshot and Delivery
Strategy: Authorize export creation and download; use a stable database snapshot or explicit per-store cutoffs and publish a manifest of scope and completion
Strengths: Makes multi-part export completeness and retry behavior auditable; avoids claiming a mixed-time dataset is atomic
Weaknesses: Long snapshots consume database resources; a PostgreSQL exported snapshot does not coordinate independent stores
When to Use: Large asynchronous tenant exports spanning multiple readers or services
Gotcha: Keep the exporting transaction open until snapshot imports complete; authorize each artifact before signing short-lived download URLs; record missing parts and clean up expired artifacts without exposing another tenant's data
